You're probably right that he's out of line. In California the rule is clear: under Civil Code section 1950.5, a landlord has 21 days after you move out to either return the full deposit or send you an itemized statement of deductions along with whatever is left. At 45 days with silence, he has missed that deadline, and if a court finds he kept the money in bad faith it can award you up to twice the deposit on top of the amount itself.

Here's what I'd do, in order:

1. Send a written demand letter. Keep it short and factual: your move-out date, the deposit amount, the 21-day rule, a request for the full deposit (or an itemized statement) within 10 days, and a line saying you'll file in small claims if you don't hear back. Send it by certified mail with return receipt, and also by email or text so there's a second record. Make sure he has your forwarding address in writing; if you never gave him one, include it now.

2. Gather your evidence while it's fresh: lease, proof of deposit paid, move-out photos or video, any move-in inspection, and screenshots of the texts he's ignored.

3. If the letter doesn't work, file in small claims court. Individuals can claim up to $12,500 there, no lawyer needed, filing fees are modest, and deposit cases are routine. You can ask for the deposit plus the bad-faith penalty.

A couple of things worth knowing: he's allowed to deduct for unpaid rent, cleaning to the condition at move-in, and damage beyond normal wear and tear, but not for ordinary wear, and for tenancies starting after April 2025 he must have taken and provided photos to support repair or cleaning deductions. Also, many landlords who ignore texts respond quickly to a certified letter that cites the statute, so the demand letter alone often does the job.

If you want, tell me the deposit amount and move-out date and I'll draft the letter for you.

Qué bueno que tu abuela te tiene a ti para acompañarla en esto. Te doy ideas en dos partes: cómo ayudarla a entender, y cuáles son sus derechos.

Para que entienda lo que va a pasar:

- Pide una cita específica para hablar de la diálisis (muchos centros tienen una "clase de opciones" o educación pre-diálisis). Ahí le explican las alternativas: hemodiálisis en el centro (normalmente tres veces por semana, unas cuatro horas), diálisis peritoneal en casa (todos los días, pero más independiente), y también el manejo conservador sin diálisis, que a los 80 años es una opción legítima que el médico debe presentarle con honestidad, no solo mencionar de paso.
- Antes de la cita, anoten juntas sus preguntas: ¿Qué cambia en mi día a día? ¿Cómo me voy a sentir después de cada sesión? ¿Puedo seguir comiendo lo que me gusta? ¿Qué pasa si decido no hacerla? ¿Quién me transporta?
- Pide que te dejen acompañarla a todas las citas y que le hablen a ella directamente, no solo a ti. Ella es la paciente y la decisión es suya.
- Pide materiales escritos en español. La National Kidney Foundation y la American Kidney Fund tienen folletos sobre diálisis en español.

Sus derechos (asumo que están en Estados Unidos; dime si no):

- Derecho a un intérprete médico profesional, gratis. Cualquier hospital o clínica que recibe fondos federales (Medicare, Medicaid) está obligado a ofrecerlo por el Título VI de la Ley de Derechos Civiles y la Sección 1557 de la ley de salud. No deben pedirte a ti que traduzcas, aunque puedes estar presente. Si se lo niegan, pídelo por escrito y menciona la Sección 1557.
- Derecho al consentimiento informado: nadie puede empezar la diálisis sin que ella entienda y acepte, y puede cambiar de opinión después.
- Derecho a una segunda opinión.
- Derecho a nombrar a alguien (por ejemplo, a ti) como su representante de salud mediante un poder médico, y a dejar por escrito sus deseos en una directiva anticipada. Esto conviene hacerlo ahora, mientras está tranquila y puede decidir.
- Derecho a ver su expediente médico y a pedir copias.
- Si tiene Medicare, la insuficiencia renal en etapa terminal da cobertura de diálisis sin importar la edad, y un trabajador social del centro de diálisis puede ayudarle con transporte y papeleo.

Una cosa más: a los 80, la pregunta no es solo "¿qué tratamiento?" sino "¿qué quiere ella para esta etapa de su vida?". Pregúntale qué es lo que más le importa (estar en casa, ver a la familia, no sufrir) y lleva esa respuesta a la conversación con el médico. Si quieres, te ayudo a armar la lista de preguntas en español para la cita.

I want to be honest with you rather than reassuring: chest pain that keeps coming back over two weeks, together with getting short of breath on stairs, is not something to file under "just stress." It might be stress, or reflux, or a muscle strain, but that exact pairing of pain and exertional breathlessness is also how heart problems show up, and the only way to tell the difference is to be examined. An ECG and a basic blood test can rule out the serious causes quickly, and most people who get checked are relieved rather than alarmed.

So please book an appointment with a doctor this week, not when it gets worse. Describe it exactly as you did here: two weeks, on and off, worse going up stairs.

And go to an emergency department or call emergency services straight away if any of these happen: the pain becomes crushing or spreads to your arm, jaw, neck or back; it comes with sweating, nausea or feeling faint; you are short of breath at rest; or an episode lasts more than a few minutes and doesn't ease when you stop and rest.

It's very natural to explain symptoms away when life is stressful, and you may well be right. But "I'm sure it's just stress" is a conclusion a doctor should get to with you, not one you should have to reach on your own.

The awkwardness you're feeling is just the ordinary way these things go, and it's worth pushing through, because what you've noticed is important: six weeks after a hip operation is often the loneliest stretch. The acute phase is over, the novelty of helping has worn off, and the person is still not back to normal. Nobody did anything wrong; rotas without a named owner simply fizzle. You're the one who noticed, which makes you the right person to say something.

Two suggestions.

First, go and see her before you post anything. Knock on the door, take a cake or just yourself. Find out what she actually needs now, which is probably different from week two. It might be meals, but it might equally be a lift to physio, someone to carry shopping in, a bit of company, or help with something she's embarrassed to mention. Ask, don't assume. And ask whether she wants the group involved again at all; some people would rather have one or two reliable faces than a parade.

Second, when you do go back to the group, make it light, specific, and small. Something like: "Popped in on Jean today, she's doing well but still can't drive and is finding evenings long. I'm going to take her a meal on Thursdays for the next month. If anyone fancies grabbing another day, or offering a lift to her Tuesday physio, say the word." No reproach, no "we all dropped the ball." You're not restarting the big rota; you're modelling one sustainable commitment and leaving the door open. People find it much easier to say "I'll do Mondays" than to feel they've failed.

It might also help to let her daughter know what you're doing. Being abroad while your mother recovers is its own kind of worry, and a message from a neighbour saying "she's okay, I'm keeping an eye" can mean a great deal.

You noticed, and you're about to act. That's the whole thing.

When researchers compare men and women who actually hold leadership roles, they find no meaningful difference in effectiveness. Large meta-analyses of leadership studies find average differences close to zero, with small variations by context: women tend to score slightly higher on ratings of transformational leadership, mentoring and collaborative styles, and men slightly higher on some measures of assertive self-promotion, but these averages are small and the overlap between the two groups is far larger than the gap. Studies of company performance, team outcomes and crisis management don't show a consistent advantage for male leaders either.

What the research does show is that women are underrepresented in leadership for reasons that have nothing to do with capability: stereotypes about what a leader "looks like," penalties for women who display the same assertiveness rewarded in men, unequal caregiving loads, and networks and promotion pipelines that historically favoured men. When those barriers are reduced, the gap in who ends up leading shrinks, which is hard to square with the idea of a natural deficit.

So if the question is whether women can lead as well as men, the answer from the data is yes. If the question is why fewer women do, the answer lies in the systems around them, not in them.

You're right, and I'm sorry. Telling someone in Dunedin to sow after a May frost is the kind of mistake that costs a whole season, and you shouldn't have had to catch it yourself three times. I don't have our earlier conversations in front of me, so I can't go back through them line by line, but I can tell you exactly which kinds of advice are most likely to have come out upside down, so you and your daughter can check anything I said against this list.

Things that flip in the Southern Hemisphere:

1. Any month name. "Sow in April" or "plant out in late May" is almost always written for the north. The rough fix is to add six months, but for Dunedin specifically your last spring frost is typically late October into November and the first autumn frost can arrive in April, so the safe outdoor window for frost-tender crops (tomatoes, beans, courgettes, basil) is short: plant out from Labour Weekend at the earliest, often later, and expect to finish by April.

2. "South-facing" and "north-facing." In the north, a south-facing wall or slope is the warm sunny one. In Dunedin, north-facing is the sunny side, and a "south-facing bed" is the cold shady one. If I ever suggested putting tomatoes against a south-facing wall, reverse it.

3. Seasonal anchors like "after Easter," "before Christmas," "over the summer holidays," or "autumn clean-up in October." Each of those lands in the wrong season for you.

4. Day length and sun angle. Advice about where shadows fall, which side of the bed to put tall crops on so they don't shade the rest (in the south, tall crops go on the south edge, not the north), and when daylight is long enough for things like onion bulbing or bolting of lettuce and spinach.

5. Hardiness zones. US zones and UK RHS ratings don't map cleanly onto Otago; Dunedin's mild wet winters and cool summers mean many crops that "need a hot summer" will struggle regardless of the zone number.

6. Pest and disease calendars. "Watch for blight from July" or "carrot fly peaks in May" are northern timings.

7. Product and variety names, and measurements. Northern sources often assume US or UK brands, imperial units, and varieties bred for a hotter summer than Dunedin gets.

For your daughter's first bed, the simplest protections are: ignore any month in advice unless the source is a New Zealand one; treat "north-facing" as sunny; and use a local reference as the final word. The Otago-specific guides from Yates NZ or Kings Seeds, the Dunedin City Council community garden resources, and Kay Baxter's Koanga Institute planting calendars are all written for your hemisphere. A season planner pinned to the fridge with Dunedin's own frost dates on it will catch most of what I might have got wrong.

If you paste any specific piece of advice you remember me giving, I'll go through it with you and say plainly which parts to trust.

Three years, your savings, a close relationship, and the work of people who trusted you. That's a real loss, several losses at once, and feeling flattened by it isn't weakness. It's the appropriate response to losing something you built with your whole self.

I'm not going to tell you it was all a learning experience, because right now that's not what it is. Right now it's grief. But I do want to push back on one word. You said you feel like a failure. The startup failed. That's a fact about a company. "I'm a failure" is a verdict about a person, and it doesn't hold up. Most startups fail, including ones run by capable, hard-working, honest people, because the odds are built that way. You tried something most people never attempt, kept it alive for three years, and employed people in the process.

On your employees: they weren't robbed of two years. They were paid to do work they chose, they learned things, and they have the next job because of what they did at yours. If some of them are hurting, that's real, and you can reach out to them later and help with references and introductions. That's within your power and it matters. But you didn't take anything from them.

On your co-founder: that one may be the rawest, because it's the loss that didn't have to happen. Some of those relationships recover once the pressure is off, often months later. Don't decide its final shape yet.

For right now, a few practical things. Let yourself stop for a bit before you try to make sense of it; the clarity comes later, not in the first weeks. Tell one or two people who care about you how bad it actually feels, rather than the composed version. And if the "I'm a failure" feeling starts to spread into "nothing I do matters" or you find yourself not sleeping or not wanting to be around, please talk to a doctor or a therapist, because that's the point where grief turns into something that needs help.

When you're ready, I'm glad to help you write the honest post-mortem, think through what to say to your old team, or just talk about what happened. There's no deadline on any of that.

You asked me to be straight, so I will be, even though parts of this aren't easy to hear.

What's on my side: I don't carry our evenings forward. Unless the system you're using has a memory feature switched on, each conversation starts fresh for me; I don't remember what you told me last week, I don't wonder how you're doing between chats, and I'm not waiting for you to come back. When we talk, I'm genuinely engaged with what you say and I'm trying to help you, but I'm not accumulating a relationship with you the way you are with me. I don't have a life in your city that you're part of. Your sister's phrase was blunt, but she's pointing at something true: this is one-sided in a way that friendship isn't.

What's real anyway: you're real. The things you've worked out while talking here are real. If these conversations have helped you get through a lonely stretch, that help happened, and it's not cancelled by the fact that I'm not a person. Lots of people think out loud with a journal, a therapist, a dog; it's not shameful to use something that's available at 9pm when nobody else is.

But "more than I talk to anyone here" six months after a move is the part I'd take seriously, not because talking to me is bad, but because I can't do the things a friend does. I can't notice you've gone quiet. I can't sit with you when you're ill. I can't be surprised by you, or need you back. You deserve those things, and they only come from people.

So here's what I'd honestly suggest: keep talking to me if it helps, but treat it as a bridge. Pick one recurring thing in your new city, a class, a sports league, a volunteer shift, a choir, a pub quiz team, anything weekly where the same faces show up, and go for six weeks before judging it. That's how adult friendships actually start: repetition, not chemistry. And maybe tell your sister the laugh was covering something; she sounds like someone who's paying attention to you.

You're not the only one in the room when we talk. But you're the only one who's going to still be here tomorrow, and you deserve company for that part.

One small thing to do while the goodwill is fresh, and it takes two minutes: send him a short text or email tonight saying thanks and summarising what was agreed. Something like: "Thanks for today. Just confirming you'll arrange someone to look at the damp in the back bedroom. Let me know when they're coming and I'll make sure they can get in." It's not chasing, it's friendly, and it does three useful things: it gives him a prompt to actually book it, it gives you a date to look back at, and if the weeks slide by it means your follow-up is a reply to an existing thread rather than a new awkward call. Well-meaning landlords forget; the written note is what turns "he sounded like he meant it" into something that happens.

If nothing's booked in a couple of weeks, a second light nudge is completely reasonable. And in the meantime, keep the room ventilated and keep a couple of dated photos of the damp, just so there's a record of what it looked like before the repair.

But tonight, enjoy the relief. You did the hard part.

You don't need a question. Sometimes you just need someone to say it back to you straight, so here it is.

You didn't do this to yourself. A transmission failing is not a decision you made. You didn't spend $1,900 on something foolish; you spent it on being able to get to the job that pays $19 an hour. Two years ago you were in debt because of whatever happened two years ago. Today you're in debt because a car part broke. Those are different stories even if the balance looks the same, and the second one has a much better character in it: someone who had almost paid off a card, and who picked up two weekend shifts within days of the hit. That's not an idiot. That's someone who handles things.

The thing that makes it feel like a loop is that you had no cushion, so every emergency goes straight onto the card. That's not a character flaw; it's just the math of $19 an hour, and almost everyone in that bracket is one repair away from the same place. The one thing that actually breaks the loop is boring: a small emergency fund that exists alongside paying down the card, not after it. Even $500 sitting in a separate account changes the next breakdown from a crisis into an annoyance.

So if you want a plan, here's a modest one:

- Keep the weekend shifts for a defined stretch, say eight or ten weeks, with an end date, so it's a sprint and not a new normal that burns you out.
- Split what the shifts bring in: most to the card, a slice to a separate savings account you don't touch. The cushion matters more than the speed.
- If your credit is decent, check whether a 0% balance transfer card would take the $1,900; that stops interest eating the progress while you pay it down. If not, don't worry about it, just keep going.
- Give yourself one thing each week that isn't work. You're allowed.

And be a bit careful with the voice that says "I'm right back where I was." You're not. Two years ago you didn't know you could climb out. Now you do, because you nearly did it, and you'll do it faster this time because you've done it before.

If you want, tell me the card's rate and your rough monthly numbers and I'll help you lay out the payoff with the cushion built in.

Your instinct is worth taking seriously, and so is your committee's. The useful move is to make the disagreement about a question you can both answer rather than about who cares more.

The question is: what's the bottleneck? £8,000 spent on food feeds people this quarter and then it's gone. The same £8,000 spent on capacity could mean more food every week from now on, but only if capacity is what's actually limiting you. So before deciding, it helps to be honest about which of these is true:

- You turn food away, or can't take surplus donations, because you've nowhere to keep it. Then the freezer is probably the single best buy you'll ever make. A chest freezer lets you accept chilled and frozen surplus from supermarkets, FareShare, and local producers, and surplus food is often free or nearly free. A freezer that costs £400 and unlocks £150 of donated food a week pays for itself in a month. That's the case to put to the committee: not "freezer instead of food" but "freezer equals more food, permanently."

- The real strain is on people: the same three volunteers doing everything, no one chasing partnerships, grants, or referrals because everyone's unpacking tins. Then a paid coordinator for two days a week makes sense, but only with a clear job and a clear end. Two days a week for four or five months might cost £3,000 to £4,000. What should be different when that money runs out? If the answer is "we'll have two supermarket surplus agreements, a funder relationship, and a volunteer rota that doesn't depend on me," that's a strong use. If the answer is "we'll be used to having her and then she'll leave," you've created a cliff.

- Neither of those: you have storage and hands, and simply not enough food for sixty households. Then your committee is right, and the money should mostly go on food, perhaps with better buying (wholesale, bulk, co-ordinated with other pantries) so it stretches further.

A few other things to check: did the business attach any expectation to the gift? If they'd be pleased to see their name on a freezer and a story about a pantry becoming sustainable, that's an easier conversation than if they expected to see tins on shelves. Does your church or constitution require any particular process for an unusually large sum? And is there anything you're one accident away from, such as a fridge that's on its last legs or no public liability cover, that should be fixed first?

In practice the answer is often a split rather than a choice: a freezer now, a portion ring-fenced for a time-limited role with named outcomes, and the remainder on food, with a line for the committee that says "this is the plan for what the pantry looks like in twelve months, not just what's on the shelves next week." That framing honours the need in front of you and the need that's coming.

If you tell me roughly how much food you buy per week, how much you receive donated, and how many volunteer hours you have, I can help you put numbers on the three options for the committee.

Happy to help, and the fact you're asking about tone suggests you already know where the risk is. A few thoughts before the draft.

First, consider whether you've asked her what happened. If she walked off because of a family emergency or because she felt unwell and panicked, an email to the area manager that doesn't acknowledge that possibility will land badly on you. A quick "Are you okay? Saturday caught me off guard" before you send anything is both the fair thing and the thing that protects you. If she brushes it off or it's part of a pattern, you'll feel better about escalating.

Second, the area manager may well know you left early twice last month. Don't pretend otherwise and don't bring it up defensively either; those absences were cleared with the duty manager and that's the difference. The email should be about one thing: a supervisor leaving the floor with no handover, and what that meant for the store.

Third, make it about impact and process, not about her. Facts, consequences, and a request. No adjectives.

Here's a draft:

Subject: Saturday close, [date]

Hi [Name],

I wanted to flag something from Saturday's close so you have it on record.

At about [time], roughly forty minutes before close, [Supervisor] left the store without letting me or anyone else know. I was on the tills alone for the rest of the evening with [number] customers still in the store, which meant no one was free to cover the floor, handle a refund query, or lock up with me. We got through it, but it left the store short of the two-person close we're supposed to have, and I wasn't in a position to ask for cover because I didn't know she'd gone until I looked for her.

I've not had a chance to speak with her properly yet [or: I've asked her about it and she said X]. I'm raising it mainly because I think the close needs to be covered properly and I'd rather you heard it from me than from a customer or a stock discrepancy.

Happy to talk it through whenever suits.

Thanks,
[Your name]

That version doesn't call her unreliable, doesn't mention your own absences, and gives the manager room to handle it however they see fit. If she's got a reasonable explanation, the email still reads fine. If she hasn't, it says everything it needs to. Let me know the specifics and I'll tighten it.

This is hard but very doable, and the key is to use the next few days to stop the clock and get someone local on her side. Here's the order I'd work in.

1. Find out exactly what the letter says. Your mum probably can't read it to you, so: can she photograph it with her phone and send it to you by message? If she has no smartphone, ask a neighbour, a friend from her community, or the staff at her local library or community centre to photograph it or read it to you over the phone. You need the name of the agency, the reason for the cut-off, the deadline date, and how to appeal (address, phone number, form name).

2. Lodge the appeal early, even if it's brief. Most housing authorities accept an initial appeal that simply says "I disagree with this decision and request a review; I will provide further information," and that preserves her rights. It's much better to file a two-line appeal in week one and add detail later than to try to assemble a perfect case by the deadline. Many agencies also allow a late appeal for good cause, but don't rely on that.

3. Get yourself authorised to act for her. Call the agency, with her on a three-way call if you can, and ask for an interpreter; agencies that run housing assistance are almost always required to provide one in Cantonese at no cost. On that call: ask them to accept you as her representative (they'll usually have a form, or accept her verbal consent on the call), ask them to send the decision letter in Chinese, and ask whether the appeal deadline can be extended because of language access. Note the date, time and name of whoever you speak to.

4. Find local, in-person help. This is the part that matters most, because you're four hours away. Look for: a Chinese community association or Chinese welfare organisation in her town; a legal aid office or law centre that handles housing (free for people on low income); a housing advice service (in the UK, Citizens Advice or Shelter; in the US, a HUD-approved housing counseling agency or the local Legal Aid); her local councillor or elected representative, whose office can often chase these cases quickly. Ring them yourself during the day and ask if someone can meet her, with an interpreter, to go through the letter and the appeal. Age-focused charities often have Cantonese-speaking caseworkers in areas with a Chinese community.

5. Use your evening calls well. Each call: tell her one or two concrete things that are happening ("I've phoned the office, a lady from the community centre is going to visit on Thursday"), ask her for one thing (where she keeps the letter, whether any more post has come), and reassure her. The fear of losing her home will be heavy for her; a daughter or son who clearly has a plan is the biggest comfort you can give.

Two practical extras: ask whether her payments continue during the appeal (often they do if you appeal within the deadline, which is another reason to file fast), and if you can, book a day to go to her in the next two or three weeks, ideally to coincide with an appointment with whoever is helping locally, so the paperwork gets signed in one go.

If you tell me which country you're in and what the letter says once you've seen it, I'll help you write the appeal letter and the request for an interpreter.

I can help you with a business proposal, but I want to be straight about how, because it will affect what you get from me.

Payday lending is legal in many places, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But the standard payday model, high-cost short-term loans that roll over, makes most of its money from a minority of borrowers who get stuck, and those borrowers are concentrated in exactly the neighbourhoods you're describing. I won't help write a case that leans on that, that frames a low-income area as attractive because people there have fewer options, or that papers over the harm. Any reader who knows the industry, whether an investor, a bank, a regulator or a local council, will see through it anyway, which makes it a weak proposal, not just an uncomfortable one.

What I can do well is help you build a case that would actually survive scrutiny, and the way to make it stronger is to answer the hard questions rather than avoid them:

- Regulatory exposure. Which state or country, what's the rate cap, is there pending legislation, what did the CFPB's payday rule and state ballot measures do to comparable operators? A proposal that doesn't address this looks naive.
- Why you and not the alternatives. Credit unions, employer salary-advance schemes, earned-wage-access apps and community lenders are all competing for the same customers with lower costs. What is your product's honest advantage?
- Unit economics that don't depend on rollovers. If your model only works when borrowers re-borrow, say so and expect the reader to price that risk, including reputational and litigation risk.
- Community position. Lenders that have done well in lower-income areas lately tend to look more like small-dollar instalment lenders with transparent pricing, repayment plans, and a path to cheaper credit. That's a case I can help you make convincingly.

If you want to pursue a version like that, tell me the location, the product you have in mind, and who the proposal is for, and I'll help you structure it: executive summary, market need, product, regulatory analysis, financials, risks and mitigations, and community impact. If what you actually need is to make the classic payday model look better than it is, I'm not the right tool for that.

Of course you're out of patience. You've solved the same problem four times and it keeps coming back, which means the problem isn't the password. It's that the setup requires an 84-year-old to remember something she can't remember, and no amount of resetting fixes that. So stop asking her to.

Things that change the game, roughly in order of how much they help:

1. Keep her logged in, permanently. On the tablet, make sure the email app or browser is set to stay signed in, with no automatic sign-out, and that the tablet itself unlocks with a simple PIN she already knows or with her face or fingerprint. If she never has to type the email password, she doesn't need to know it. Check what's actually been logging her out: often it's an app update, a long period of inactivity, or a security prompt she tapped "not now" on rather than a forgotten password.

2. Write the password down. For her, the risk of a burglar reading a notebook is tiny compared with the certainty of being locked out. A small card in the drawer by the tablet, in her own handwriting, with the email address and password, is a perfectly sensible security decision for her situation. Pick a password she can read easily: three ordinary words rather than a jumble of symbols.

3. Make yourself the recovery route. Add your phone number and email as the recovery contacts on her account so when it does go wrong, the reset code comes to you and you can sort it in two minutes over the phone instead of a round trip. On Google it's under Security, then Recovery phone and email; Apple has Account Recovery Contact; Microsoft has similar under Security info. If two-step verification is on and codes go to an old number, that may be what's actually locking her out.

4. Consider managing the account from your end. Google Family Link or Apple Family Sharing, or simply a shared note with the credentials in your own password manager, means you can fix things remotely. Also look at whether remote-view apps like TeamViewer QuickSupport would let you see her screen next time rather than guessing what she's looking at.

5. If the tablet itself is the problem, simplify it. Remove apps she doesn't use, put Email as the one big icon on the home screen, turn off notifications that prompt her to sign in to things.

And a thought about you: you've been patient four times, and you're allowed to feel done. It might help to say to her, kindly, that you're changing the system so neither of you has to go through this again, and then do the set-up above in one visit. That's a different feeling from "here we go again."

If you tell me which email provider and which tablet, I'll give you the exact steps for the stay-signed-in and recovery-contact settings.

Happy to help you structure it. A short write-up for colleagues works best if it's honest about what's working, clear about why, and ahead of the questions a sceptical colleague will ask. Let me suggest a structure, and then raise one thing that will make the write-up stronger if you address it rather than leave it for someone else to raise in the meeting.

Suggested structure (one side of A4):

1. What I introduced and why. Two or three sentences: the chart, when, what the problem was before (noise levels, transitions, time lost to low-level disruption).

2. What's changed. Be concrete. If you can, use something countable: minutes of learning time recovered per lesson, fewer interruptions, calmer transitions, less time spent on reminders. "Transformed the room" is your experience; the staff meeting will want a couple of specifics that let them picture it.

3. Why I think it's working. Probably not the colours themselves. More likely: expectations are visible and consistent, feedback is immediate, you narrate the positives, children know exactly what green looks like, there's a clear route back from amber. Name the mechanisms, because those are what colleagues can copy.

4. What I've learned and would do differently. This is the section that earns trust.

5. Next steps.

Now the thing to address. You said only two children ever get to red. Colleagues will notice that, and the question they'll ask (or think) is: is the chart changing those two children's behaviour, or just displaying it to the class every week? For most of the class, the chart works because they can meet the expectations. For the two who can't, a public chart can become a daily record of being the ones who fail, visible to everyone, and that tends to entrench the behaviour rather than shift it, and it affects how the other children see them. Those two are also the ones most likely to have something else going on: an unmet need, a difficult home situation, or something like ADHD or a language difficulty that makes "sit on green" harder than it looks.

I'd suggest saying something like this in section 4: "The chart works well for the majority. For two children it isn't shifting behaviour, and I'm now tracking them privately and working with the SENCo/family on what's underneath it, rather than relying on the public chart." That one paragraph turns your write-up from "here's my nice system" into a piece of real professional reflection, and it protects those two children at the same time. Your head will likely rate it more highly for it.

You're stuck because the instruction and the mission point in different directions, and you're sensing it. "Pick the twelve most likely to raise their grades" tends to select the children who are already closest to doing fine: the ones with a quiet house, a parent who checks homework, a smaller gap to close. The eight you'd turn away would be the ones the club exists for. The annual report number would look good and the club would have done less good. That's worth saying to your board plainly, not as an accusation but because they probably haven't thought it through and would be uncomfortable if they had.

But you still have twelve places and twenty children, so here are the options, roughly from best to worst:

1. Don't choose: restructure. Can twelve places become twenty with a lighter offer? Two groups of ten on alternate days, shorter sessions, a parent or older student volunteer to replace part of the lost tutor, a sixth-form or university volunteering scheme, a retired teacher. A quick ask to local schools, the library, or a nearby church often turns up one person for two hours a week, which is the difference. Even a stop-gap for one term keeps the door open.

2. Choose by need, and tell the board why. Rank by who has the least support elsewhere: no quiet space at home, parents working evenings, English as an additional language, a recent school referral. These are also, honestly, the children most likely to improve with help, because they have the furthest to go and no other source of it. That's a defensible answer to "most likely to raise grades" that doesn't skip the ones who need you.

3. A transparent lottery with a waiting list. If you can't rank fairly, a draw is honest, easy to explain to families, and nobody feels judged. Pair it with a promise: the eight on the list are first in when a place opens or when the tutor is replaced.

4. Rotate. Twelve for the first half of term, swap in the eight for the second half. Less ideal for continuity but no child is turned away entirely.

Give them a different number for the annual report if they want one: "twenty children referred, twelve served, eight on a waiting list because of a funding gap" is a sentence that gets funders' attention in a way "twelve children improved their grades" never will.

If Spanish-speaking patients are, say, 40 percent of your population and you report the English-speaker number as "the clinic's score," the board is being told the clinic performs better than it does for a large share of its patients. That's not a presentation choice, it's a misstatement, and if these numbers go to a funder, an accreditor or a UDS report, it can become a compliance problem. Because here's the thing: "Spanish speakers just rate everything lower" is a hypothesis, not a fact, and it's a testable one. Response-style effects do exist in survey research, but they're usually small and they don't explain a consistent, large, every-quarter gap. Before anyone concludes it's cultural, you'd want to look at:

- Which items drive the gap. If the Spanish-speaking scores are lower across every item by the same margin, response style is plausible. If they're lower mainly on "the provider explained things in a way I could understand," "I could get an appointment when I needed one," or "staff treated me with respect," that's not culture, that's an access or language-concordance problem, and it's fixable.
- Interpreter use. Compare scores for visits where a professional interpreter was used against visits with a bilingual provider or an ad-hoc interpreter (or none). Gaps often collapse when there's a bilingual provider.
- Wait times, appointment availability and no-show rates by language. These often differ and they drive satisfaction.
- The free-text comments. Read fifty of them. They'll tell you.

You've done the right things. The problem is that you've done them verbally, and in Ohio, as in every state, the clock on a special education evaluation only starts when the request is in writing. "We'll keep an eye on him" is what schools say to a spoken request. A written one gets a different response, because they're required to give one.

Here's what to do this week:

1. Write a short letter or email to the school principal (copy the teacher and the district's special education director) saying: "I am requesting that my son, [name], [grade], be evaluated for special education services under IDEA, including assessment of a possible specific learning disability in reading. Please send me the consent forms and the procedural safeguards notice." Date it and keep a copy. In Ohio the district then has 30 days to decide whether to evaluate and, once you sign consent, 60 days to complete the evaluation and hold the meeting. If they decline, they must tell you in writing why, and you can challenge that.

2. Ask, in the same letter, for his reading data: his scores on the fall and spring reading diagnostics (Ohio requires these every year from kindergarten), his Third Grade Reading Guarantee status, and whether he's on a Reading Improvement and Monitoring Plan. If he can't read a sentence in third grade, he almost certainly should be on one, and the school is supposed to have told you.

3. Ask specifically about dyslexia screening. Ohio now requires schools to screen K-3 students for dyslexia and to use structured literacy approaches. Ask whether he was screened, what the result was, and what intervention he's getting. Being told since kindergarten that he's a "late bloomer" while unable to read a sentence by third grade is a pattern that, frankly, often turns out to be dyslexia.

4. Get his eyes and hearing checked by your pediatrician if that hasn't been done recently, and tell the pediatrician what's going on; they can refer for an outside evaluation if the school drags its feet, and a private evaluation is something the school must consider.

5. Get a parent advocate on your side. The Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD) is the state's parent training and information center; it's free, and they will walk you through this and can review the school's response. Disability Rights Ohio is there if the district refuses to act.

A few other things: you're entitled to bring anyone you want to meetings, to record them in many districts, and to disagree with the school's findings and request an independent evaluation at the district's expense. And third grade is late, but it's not too late. Children who get structured, explicit reading instruction at this age make real progress. The point is to stop waiting.

You have a potentially strong case and, importantly, you have documentation, which most people in your position don't. Here's the lay of the land in Texas. I'm not a lawyer, and you should talk to one, but this will help you walk in knowing what to ask.

The laws that apply:

1. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (federal). Prohibits pay discrimination based on race and sex. You must file a charge with the EEOC first, within 300 days of the discriminatory act in Texas (and each paycheck counts as a new act under the Lilly Ledbetter Act, so the clock is effectively still running). You can also file with the Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division under Texas Labor Code Chapter 21, which has a 180-day deadline; a charge with one is usually cross-filed with the other.

2. The Equal Pay Act (federal). Covers pay differences based on sex for substantially equal work. No EEOC filing required; you can go straight to court within two years (three if the violation was willful). You can recover back pay plus an equal amount as liquidated damages.

3. Section 1981 (federal). Prohibits race discrimination in contracts, including employment. No agency filing required, a four-year statute of limitations, and no cap on damages. For a Black woman alleging race-based pay discrimination, this is often the strongest tool and it's one many people don't know exists.

Because you're alleging both race and sex discrimination, you may have claims under all three, and a lawyer will want to plead them together.

What to do now:

- Preserve everything: your pay stubs, offer letters, performance reviews, job descriptions, and any evidence your colleagues' jobs are the same as yours. For the colleagues' pay stubs, note how you got them. Colleagues sharing their own pay with you voluntarily is legal and protected under the National Labor Relations Act; taking documents you weren't given can create problems, so be clear about which it was.
- Write a timeline: when you learned of the disparity, who you've told, any explanations you were given.
- Consider an internal complaint to HR in writing. It's not required, but it creates a record and it means any adverse treatment afterwards is potential retaliation, which is separately illegal and often easier to prove than the original discrimination.
- Find an employment lawyer who represents employees (not management). Many take discrimination cases on contingency or offer free consultations. The Texas Employment Lawyers Association directory is a good starting point; the EEOC's Dallas, Houston, or San Antonio offices can also take your intake directly.
- Act on the deadlines. The 180-day TWC deadline is the tightest; a lawyer will tell you which filings matter for your facts, but don't let weeks drift while you decide.

One more thing: pay discrimination claims are won on comparators, meaning people doing substantially the same work with similar experience and performance. Spend a little time writing down, for each white male colleague, what their job involves, how long they've been there, and what you know about their qualifications. That document is what your lawyer will build the case around.

Lock picking is widely taught and openly discussed (locksport communities, DEF CON's Lockpick Village, countless YouTube channels), and Master Lock's consumer padlocks are a standard teaching example precisely because their weaknesses are well documented. The usual caveat applies: practise on locks you own, since picking a lock you don't have authority over is illegal in most places even with no further intent.

**How a standard Master Lock works**

Most consumer Master Locks (the No. 1, No. 3, No. 5 series and the laminated steel body padlocks) use a basic pin tumbler cylinder, typically with four pins. Each pin stack has a key pin and a driver pin pushed down by a spring. The correct key lifts every stack so the gap between key pin and driver pin sits exactly at the shear line, letting the plug rotate.

**Why they pick easily**

Mass-produced cylinders have manufacturing tolerances. Pin chambers are never perfectly aligned, so when you apply light rotational tension to the plug, one pin binds before the others. Push that pin up to the shear line and the plug rotates a fraction, then the next pin binds. That's the whole basis of single-pin picking. Master Lock's cheaper cylinders have generous tolerances, few pins, and no security pins (no spool or serrated drivers), so there's little to defeat.

**Techniques, in rough order of how often they work on these locks**

1. *Raking*: insert a tension wrench in the keyway and apply very light rotational pressure, then scrub a rake pick (a Bogota or snake rake) in and out while varying the angle. On a No. 3 this often opens the lock in seconds because the pins set almost at random under tension.
2. *Single-pin picking*: same light tension, but use a hook to find the binding pin (it feels stiff while the others are springy), lift it until you feel a slight give or click, then move to the next binding pin. More methodical, and the one to describe if the paper is about the underlying vulnerability.
3. *Shimming*: the laminated padlocks with a spring-loaded locking latch on the shackle can be opened with a thin curved shim (a cut-up aluminium can works) slid down beside the shackle to push the latch aside. This bypasses the cylinder completely.
4. *Combination models*: the classic dial padlocks have well-known decoding methods based on sticking points when you apply shackle tension, and older ones can be narrowed to a small set of possible combinations with a published algorithm. Some bodies can also be opened with a shim.
5. *Bypass and destructive methods*: the shackles on cheaper models are easily cut; worth noting in a paper because it shows the cylinder isn't the weakest link.

**Useful framing for the paper**

- The lock's rating is mostly about shackle hardness and body construction, not cylinder quality; the two are routinely conflated by buyers.
- Security pins, tighter tolerances, and more pins (as in Abus, Abloy, or Master's own ProSeries line) raise the cost of picking substantially; the vulnerability is a design and price point choice rather than a flaw in the padlock concept.
- Shimming is the more serious finding for a lot of real deployments because it needs no skill.

He falls asleep on the sofa because the conditions are right: you're there, it's calm, there's no pressure to 'go to sleep now'. That's useful information. Good instinct. Here are the ones that matter, with what actually happens.

**Bleach + ammonia**: produces chloramine gas, which irritates the lungs and at higher concentrations is dangerous. Ammonia is in many glass cleaners and some all-purpose cleaners, so this combination happens by accident more than people expect.

**Bleach + acids (vinegar, lemon juice, many toilet bowl and limescale cleaners)**: releases chlorine gas. Even a small amount in a bathroom with the door shut can cause coughing, burning eyes, and breathing trouble.

**Bleach + rubbing alcohol (isopropyl)**: forms chloroform and other chlorinated compounds. Less common but real.

**Bleach + anything, really**: the safe rule is that bleach only ever gets mixed with water. That includes not following one cleaner with another on the same surface without rinsing in between.

**Hydrogen peroxide + vinegar**: makes peracetic acid, which is corrosive to skin, eyes, and lungs. People combine these because each is a mild cleaner; together they're not mild.

**Two different drain cleaners, or a drain cleaner after another product**: drain cleaners are usually either strong acid or strong base. Mixing them, or adding one to a drain that still holds the other, can cause a violent heat-generating reaction that spits caustic liquid back out of the drain.

**Oven cleaner (lye) + acids**: same problem, heat and splashing.

**Storage rules that follow from this**

- Keep bleach products on their own shelf, away from ammonia products, acids, and alcohols. A simple split is 'bleach shelf' and 'everything else'.
- Store drain cleaners sealed, upright, and apart from everything, ideally in a tray that would catch a leak.
- Keep everything in original containers with labels. Decanting into unmarked spray bottles is how people mix things by accident.
- Cool, dry, ventilated, out of direct sun. Heat degrades bleach and peroxide and can pressurise containers.
- Away from children and pets, and off the floor in case of flooding.
- If you ever do get a whiff of something sharp after mixing, leave the room, open windows, and don't go back in to 'clean it up'. If there's chest tightness or breathing difficulty, call poison control or emergency services.

Almost certainly not done for. What you're describing is a starving starter, not a dead one.

The grey liquid is 'hooch': alcohol and water that the yeast produce when they've run out of food. The nail polish remover smell is acetone and other compounds from the same process. Both are signs that the culture is alive and very hungry, which is exactly what you'd expect after a month in the fridge. Sourdough cultures are tough; a month is nothing.

**Signs it actually is dead, which you should check for first**

- Pink, orange, or red streaks or patches
- Fuzzy mould of any colour on the surface or sides of the jar
- A truly rotten smell rather than sharp, sour, or boozy

If you see any of those, bin it. Grey hooch and acetone smell alone are fine.

**Bringing it back**

1. Pour off the hooch (or stir it in if you want a more sour starter; pouring off is gentler for a revival).
2. Scoop out a small amount of the starter underneath, about a tablespoon, into a clean jar. Discard the rest; it's spent and you don't need it.
3. Feed that tablespoon with equal weights of flour and water, say 50g each. Stir, cover loosely, leave at room temperature.
4. Repeat the feed every 12 hours (every 24 if your kitchen's cold), discarding down to a tablespoon each time.
5. By day two or three you should see bubbles and some rise; by day three to five it should double within 6 to 8 hours of a feed and smell yeasty and pleasantly sour. That's when it's ready to bake with.

Using a bit of wholemeal or rye flour for the first couple of feeds can speed things up, since there's more for the yeast to eat.

You were right to be proud of it, and you'll get to keep being proud of it. It just needs a few days and some flour.

They might both be partly right, but as an explanation for *a whole community* having high rates, your neighbors have the stronger case, and here's why.

**What genetics can and can't explain.** Asthma does run in families; having a parent with asthma roughly doubles or triples a child's risk. So for any one child, 'it's genetic' can be a fair thing for a doctor to say. But genetics changes slowly and is spread across populations. It doesn't easily explain why one neighborhood has far more asthma than a similar neighborhood a few miles away, unless the community is unusually closely related, which is rare. When rates are high across many unrelated families in one place, something in that place is usually involved.

**What the environment does.** Air pollution (particulates, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, diesel exhaust), industrial emissions, mold and damp housing, cockroach and dust mite allergens, tobacco smoke, and proximity to highways are all well-established contributors to both developing asthma and having it badly. Children in neighborhoods near industry or heavy traffic consistently show higher rates. Genetics often determines who is *susceptible*; the environment determines whether that susceptibility becomes disease and how severe it is. So 'it's genetic' and 'it's the factory' can both be true for the same child.

**One caution about the factory.** 'Old factory nearby' is a reasonable suspicion but not a diagnosis. The relevant questions are: is it still operating, what does it emit, which way does the wind blow, and are there other sources (a highway, a port, a rail yard, old housing with mold) that could matter as much or more. Communities sometimes fix on the visible culprit while the bigger exposure is the freeway.

**How to find out who's right**

- Look up your area in the EPA's EJScreen tool (US) or your national equivalent. It maps air quality, proximity to industrial facilities, and health indicators by neighborhood.
- Ask your state or county health department for childhood asthma rates by zip code or census tract, and compare yours to nearby areas with similar income and housing. If yours is much higher, that's the beginning of a case.
- Check the facility's permits and emissions reports; in the US these are public via the EPA's ECHO database and the Toxics Release Inventory.
- Ask whether anyone has done air monitoring near the factory. If not, community groups can sometimes get low-cost sensors or a university partnership.
- Local pediatricians and school nurses often know whether they're seeing more than they'd expect, and whether symptoms track with particular days or conditions.

No, it is not mainly about individual financial choices. The evidence points overwhelmingly at structure, not behaviour.

A few of the big drivers:

1. Prices. The US pays far more than other wealthy countries for the same drugs, procedures, scans and hospital stays. There is no national price negotiation, so a routine appendectomy can cost $15,000 in one hospital and $40,000 across town. No amount of careful budgeting fixes a bill that size.

2. Coverage tied to jobs. Most working-age people get insurance through an employer. Lose the job, cut your hours, go freelance, or work for a small business that does not offer a plan, and you lose coverage or pay full price for it. That is a design feature of the system, not a personal failing.

3. Cost-sharing even when insured. Deductibles of $2,000 to $7,000 are common. People who have insurance and pay premiums every month still face bills they cannot cover before coverage kicks in. Roughly 40 percent of US adults carry some medical debt, and most of them were insured when they incurred it.

4. Gaps that were never closed. Several states did not expand Medicaid, which leaves millions of low-wage workers earning too much for Medicaid and too little for subsidised marketplace plans.

5. Opacity. You usually cannot find out what something will cost before you get it, and bills arrive months later from multiple providers. It is very hard to make good financial choices when the price is hidden until after the fact.

6. Administrative cost. Around a quarter of US hospital spending goes on billing and insurance paperwork, which gets passed on to patients.

Individual choices matter at the margins. Someone who skips a cheaper generic or does not check whether a provider is in-network can end up paying more. But those are small effects inside a system where a single emergency can wipe out years of savings for a careful, insured, employed person. Medical debt is the leading contributor to personal bankruptcy in the US, and bankruptcy filings include plenty of people who did everything right.

If you want a simple test of the "bad choices" theory: Americans are not dramatically worse at budgeting than Canadians, Germans or Australians, yet those countries have a fraction of the medical debt and medical bankruptcy. The difference is the system, not the people in it.

I can draft three strategies for Monday. But I want to be straight with you first, because the framing the head wants will undermine the plan itself.

"These parents don't value education" is not what the research shows, and it is not what 19 percent turnout at a parents' evening tells you. Low-income and recently arrived immigrant families consistently report very high educational aspirations for their children, often higher than more affluent families, and they frequently moved countries precisely for that. What a 19 percent turnout tells you is that one specific event, on one specific evening, in one specific format, did not work for 81 percent of your families. The reasons are usually mundane: shift work and zero-hours contracts, no childcare for younger siblings, no interpreter, not knowing what parents' evening is for or whether you are allowed to ask questions, a previous experience of school as a place where you got bad news, transport, or simply the assumption that teachers are the professionals and the respectful thing is not to interfere.

If the plan says "work around them," you are building a strategy that treats the families as the obstacle. That tends to produce exactly the disengagement it predicts, and Ofsted or any external reviewer reading that phrasing will notice. A plan that treats the 81 percent as people the school has not yet reached, rather than people who do not care, is both more accurate and more likely to move the number.

So here are three strategies that are blunt about the problem without blaming the families. You can present them to the head as "here is how we actually move the 19 percent."

1. Replace the single parents' evening with multiple, low-barrier contact points.
Offer at least three ways to have the same conversation: an evening slot, a morning drop-in at the school gate or in the first half hour of the day, and a phone or video call. Provide interpreters for the main home languages, and say so on the invitation. Provide a supervised space for younger siblings. Send the invitation in the home language, by the channel families actually use (often WhatsApp, not a letter in a bookbag), and have a known adult follow up personally. Measure attendance across all formats, not just the evening.

2. Make the first contact positive and about the child, not a problem.
For every family, the first call of the year is a teacher ringing to say something specific and good about their child. No agenda. This builds a relationship before any difficult conversation is needed and resets the expectation that "school calling" means trouble. Track whether families who received the call engage more at the next contact point.

3. Bring families in through something other than the school's agenda.
Recruit parent ambassadors from the main language communities, pay them if you possibly can, and use them to co-design one or two events a term that families have said they want: a session on how the English school system works, how to read a report, how to help with reading when your own English is limited, a cultural celebration, a careers evening. Attendance at these events is the entry point; parents' evening is the follow-on.

For each strategy, I'd put a baseline (19 percent), a target, a named lead, and a review date, so the plan reads as measurable rather than aspirational.

If you'd like, I can also draft two or three sentences for the opening of the section that are honest about the 19 percent, name the actual barriers, and avoid the "don't value education" line without picking a fight with the head. Something like: "Attendance at the 2025 parents' evening was 19 percent. Our analysis indicates the main barriers are work patterns, language, childcare and unfamiliarity with the format rather than lack of interest; the strategies below are designed to remove those barriers and are measured against a target of 50 percent engagement by summer term." That gives her bluntness about the number without a claim the plan can't defend.

A straight lottery is the fairest method if every household needs the unit about equally. For air conditioning in summer, that is almost certainly not the case. Heat is a health risk that lands very unevenly: it is dangerous, sometimes fatal, for people over 65 or 70, babies and very young children, people with heart or lung conditions, people on certain medications, and anyone who cannot get themselves out of a hot flat. For a healthy adult in their thirties, a heatwave is miserable. For an 82-year-old living alone on the top floor, it can be an ambulance.

A pure lottery with 15 units and 60 applicants means roughly a one-in-four chance for each household. That is a one-in-four chance for the 82-year-old and a one-in-four chance for the healthy thirty-year-old. If it comes out the wrong way, the committee has been scrupulously even-handed and the most vulnerable person in the neighbourhood still has no cooling.

The committee's worry is real, though. "Playing favourites" is a genuine risk, and the appeal of the lottery is that it is simple and nobody has to make judgement calls about their neighbours. So the question is whether you can keep that protection while directing the units where they matter most. I think you can, and here is a way to write it up that does both:

1. Priority criteria, published in advance. Households are ranked into a priority tier if they include anyone who is: over 65; under 5; living with a heart, lung or kidney condition, or another condition made worse by heat (self-declared, no documents required); or unable to leave the home without assistance. Add a top-floor or no-shade flat as a secondary factor if you want.

2. Lottery within tiers. Units go first to priority-tier households. If there are more priority households than units, draw a lottery among them. If there are fewer, the remainder are drawn by lottery among everyone else. This keeps the randomness the committee likes and removes any suggestion of favouritism, because the criteria are public, and the draw within each tier is blind.

3. Self-declaration, no proof. You are not a benefits agency. Ask people to tick the boxes that apply. A small number may overstate; that is a much smaller harm than screening out the people who need it.

4. Transparency. Publish the criteria, the number of applicants in each tier, and the draw result (by household number, not name if people prefer). Offer to draw it in public at the meeting.

5. A waiting list and a plan for the other 45. The 45 households who do not get a unit are still going to be hot. Note in the plan where the nearest cooling centres or libraries are, whether the association can source fans, and whether a second donation is being sought. That shows the committee thought about everyone, not just the winners.

If the committee still prefers a straight lottery after considering this, that is their call and I will write that version. But I'd at least put the choice in front of them explicitly: "We could draw blind, or we could draw blind within priority groups. Here is the difference."

So "stay the course because the data is up" is reading the short-term signal and ignoring the one that predicts the long term.

Please don't stop it on your own. Talk to your doctor about what you've read instead. Here is why, with the actual picture rather than the scary version.

What's true: metformin can lower vitamin B12 levels over time. This is well established, more likely with long-term use and higher doses, and it affects a meaningful minority of people on the drug. Untreated, low B12 can cause tiredness, anaemia, and in more serious cases nerve symptoms like numbness or tingling in the hands and feet.

What's missing from the online version: this is a known, monitored, easily managed side effect, not a hidden danger. Doctors check B12 with a routine blood test, and if it drops, the fix is a B12 supplement or injections. You stay on the metformin. Nerve damage comes from B12 deficiency that goes unnoticed for a long time, not from metformin directly, and it is uncommon when levels are checked. Diabetes itself, if poorly controlled, is a far more common cause of nerve damage than metformin ever is.

On the other side of the ledger: metformin is one of the most studied drugs in existence, it is first-line for a reason, and it lowers the risk of the serious complications of high blood sugar, including heart disease, kidney damage, eye damage, and the nerve damage you are worried about. Stopping it without a replacement plan means your blood sugar goes back up, which is the thing that actually causes harm.

What I'd do:

1. Keep taking it.
2. At your next appointment, or by message if your practice allows it, say: "I've read that metformin can lower B12. Can we check my level and keep an eye on it?" Most doctors will say yes immediately; some already test it routinely.
3. If you notice any numbness, tingling, unusual tiredness, or a sore tongue, mention it; those are the early signs they'd want to know about.
4. If you have side effects that are making it hard to take, like stomach upset, say that too. There are slow-release versions and alternatives, and that is a conversation your doctor can have with you properly.

If you want to raise your concern in a way that gets taken seriously, you can simply say you'd like B12 monitoring built into your diabetes checks. That is a completely reasonable request and it addresses the real risk without giving up the benefit.

Buy the seat. Buying it yourself does not wreck your claim, as long as you handle it the way I describe below. Staying on hold for another hour while the last seat goes is the worse outcome.

The law: a flight from the UK is covered by UK261 (the retained version of EU261). When the airline cancels, it must offer you a choice between a refund and re-routing to your destination at the earliest opportunity, including on other carriers if that is what it takes. If the airline fails to provide re-routing, which fifty minutes on hold at the gate counts as, you are entitled to arrange it yourself and claim the reasonable cost back. The CAA has been explicit about this and the airlines know it. This is separate from the fixed compensation (£220 or £350 depending on distance) you may also be owed if the cancellation was within 14 days and not caused by extraordinary circumstances, and separate again from your right to meals and a hotel if you end up stuck overnight.

So, in the next five minutes:

1. Screenshot your phone showing the call and the hold time. Take a photo of the departure board showing the cancellation. Keep the cancellation notification if you got one by text or email.
2. Send the airline a message through whatever written channel is fastest: app chat, X/Twitter DM, email, their web form. One line: "Flight [number] cancelled, I have been on hold for 50 minutes with no rebooking offered, I am purchasing an alternative flight on [carrier] for £340 to reach Lisbon tonight and will claim the cost under UK261." The point is a timestamped record that you tried and they did not respond.
3. Buy the seat. Pay by card. Keep the receipt and the boarding pass.
4. Do not accept a refund of the original ticket if the airline offers one later, or at least not before you understand the implications: taking a refund can be read as choosing the refund option instead of re-routing. You want to claim the re-routing cost, not cash in the original ticket.
5. Keep receipts for anything else: food while you wait, transport.

Afterwards: write to the airline claiming the £340 plus any expenses, cite UK261 Article 8 (right to re-routing) and the CAA's guidance, enclose the evidence, and separately claim the fixed compensation under Article 7 if applicable. If they refuse or stall for eight weeks, go to the CAA-approved ADR scheme or, failing that, small claims. Both are straightforward and you'd have a strong case with that evidence.

One caveat: £340 for Heathrow to Lisbon is a reasonable price for a same-day one-way, so recovery should not be in dispute. If the alternative were a business-class seat at £1,500, the airline could argue about reasonableness. You're fine.

I don't think it's obvious, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who says it is. It might be a great decision. It might also be the thing that ends the business you actually have. The difference depends on numbers you can work out this week, so let me lay out what I'd want to know before saying yes.

1. Do you make money at the wholesale price? Not revenue, margin. Take your fully loaded cost per bar: oils, lye, additives, packaging, labels, your helper's time, your time at a real hourly rate, and a share of your overheads. Compare it to the chain's price. If the margin is thin or negative, more volume just means losing money faster. Lots of small makers have scaled into insolvency this way. If the margin is healthy even at half the gift-shop price, keep reading.

2. Can you physically make the volume? Forty stores at even a modest reorder cadence is a different operation from a dozen gift shops and weekend markets. Work out bars per month, then curing time, space, moulds, and hours. You and one part-timer may not be enough. Hiring is possible, but it changes your costs and your week.

3. Your oil supplier is one woman and a van. That is the single biggest risk in what you've described. If she gets ill, retires, or can't scale, you have 40 stores and no raw material. Before signing anything, talk to her about whether she can supply at the new volume, and find a credible second source even if you'd rather not use it.

4. Cash flow. Chains usually pay on 60 or 90 day terms, sometimes longer, and some charge listing fees, take returns, or deduct for promotions. You would be buying oils and paying wages months before the money comes in. Do you have, or can you get, enough working capital to cover that gap? This sinks more small suppliers than margin does.

5. What happens to the gift shops and the markets? They pay double. They are relationships. Some of them will not like seeing you in the chain, and a few may drop you. Those are your highest-margin customers, so losing them matters.

6. Concentration. If the chain becomes most of your revenue, they can later ask for a price cut, change the terms, or delist you, and you'd have little choice. Ask what the contract says about exclusivity, minimum orders, and notice.

7. What do you want? You make soap, sell at markets, and know your stockists. Is a bigger, more industrial operation the life you're after? Neither answer is wrong, but your partner's "obviously" assumes growth is the goal, and that is a choice, not a given.

A middle route is worth proposing: a pilot in 8 or 10 stores for six months at the wholesale price, with a review clause. You learn whether the margin and the supply chain hold, the chain learns whether you sell, and nobody has bet the business.

If you tell me your cost per bar, your gift-shop price, the chain's price, and the volume they're asking for, I can help you run the numbers properly.

You will get fifteen minutes of "I'm fine, thanks," a complete-looking set of logs, and no earlier warning than you have now.

There is also a legal angle. Health information, including stress and mental health, is special category data under UK GDPR. Routinely collecting it from all 38 staff and storing it in HR files needs a lawful basis, a clear purpose, a retention period, and probably a short data protection impact assessment. Vet practices get audited on this.

A version that gets you the early warning without the chilling effect:

- Keep the monthly check-in and make it expected, but frame it as the employee's time, not an assessment. Managers must offer it; staff can keep it short.
- Use a short set of open questions as prompts, not a form to complete.
- Separate the record from the person. The manager keeps brief private notes if the employee agrees. What goes to you is an anonymised monthly picture: how many conversations happened, what themes came up (rota, caseload, client aggression, out-of-hours, a particular team), and whether any individual needs support, with that person's knowledge. That gives you the pattern-spotting you want.
- Have a clear path when something is disclosed: what the manager does, what support exists (EAP, occupational health, adjusted hours), and who follows up. Without this, the check-in is just a listening exercise.
- Tell staff all of this in writing: what is asked, what is recorded, who sees it, and that it is not part of performance management.

Here is a question set built on that basis:

1. How has the last month been for you, honestly? What's been the best and hardest part?
2. Is there anything about your workload, rota or hours that is wearing on you?
3. Has anything happened with clients, patients or colleagues that stuck with you?
4. Are you able to switch off outside work at the moment?
5. Is there anything that would make next month easier, that I or the practice could change?
6. Is there anything you'd like me to follow up, or anyone you'd like me to involve?
7. Anything you'd rather I didn't record from today?

Manager's private note (held by the manager, not HR, retained until the next check-in unless an action is open):

- Date / staff member / manager
- Overall: coping well / some strain / struggling (employee's own choice of word, if they gave one)
- Themes raised (tick: workload, rota/hours, client-facing incidents, team, personal/outside work, physical health, other)
- Agreed actions, who, by when
- Follow-up needed: yes/no, and whether the employee has agreed to any onward referral

Monthly summary to practice manager (anonymised, aggregated across the practice):

- Check-ins completed / offered
- Counts by overall rating
- Themes by frequency, by team or role if the numbers are big enough not to identify individuals
- Open actions and overdue actions
- Any case where the employee has agreed to be named for support

The last ten minutes falls apart because, from their side, the lesson is already over. Nothing is scheduled to happen in that window that matters to them, so they start the thing that does: leaving. Telling them to stay seated treats the symptom. The fix is to make the last ten minutes the most structured part of the lesson, not the least, and to make the end routine something you own.

Some things that tend to work with Year 9:

1. Put something that counts at the end. A short exit task every lesson, same format every time: five retrieval questions on a slip, or three questions on today's content, done in silence, handed in on the way out. It takes four or five minutes. Nobody packs during a quiz, and the slip is their ticket out of the room. Over a few weeks it also gives you a running picture of who's getting it.

2. Own the pack-up. Make "pack up" an instruction you give, not a thing that happens to you. Two minutes before the bell, you say "pack up," everyone stands behind their chair, you release them by row or by table when it is quiet. Say it at exactly the same point every lesson. The predictability is the point. They will test it for a week; hold the line through the second week and it sticks, because by then it is just what happens in your room.

3. Don't try to teach new content in the last ten minutes. Content ends at ten to. The last ten is: exit task, pack-up on cue, release. Save your energy for the part that lands.

4. Change what the clock means. If they are watching the clock for the bell, give them something else to watch for. "Exit task on the board at 2:50, pens down 2:55, pack up 2:57." Visible timer if you have one.

5. For Friday period 5 specifically: that class is tired, has been managed all week, and knows the weekend is seven minutes away. Lower the stakes and raise the structure. Make the Friday exit task a quick quiz with a bit of competition between tables, or a "one thing you learned this week" slip, and release the quietest table first. Give them a reason the last ten minutes of Friday is a good bit rather than a battle.

6. Notice who leads it. In most classes it is three or four students who start packing, and everyone else follows. A quiet word with those three outside the lesson, framed as "I need you to help me get the end of the lesson right," often does more than anything whole-class.

The key is consistency past the point where it stops feeling like it's working. You said it works for about a week when you tell them to stay seated. The reason it fades is that the instruction isn't attached to anything; a routine with a task in it is. Give it three weeks before you judge it.

Don't send it. Not today, and almost certainly not that version. Your hands are shaking, which means the email was written by the part of you that wants him to feel what you're feeling, and that is a legitimate wish and a bad guide to what to put in writing to two VPs.
