You are right to be angry, and you are right that it needs to be addressed. The question is how to address it so that the outcome is you getting credit, not you getting labelled as the person who sent the long, angry email.

The problem with the 600-word email to four people:

- The VPs saw a good idea presented well this morning. An email from someone they may not know, accusing the presenter and asking them to adjudicate, reads as a dispute, not as a correction. The idea becomes contested. Some of that mud sticks to you even when you are right.
- Your manager is being told, in front of their bosses, that they didn't know what their own team member was working on. They will not thank you for that, even if they take your side.
- It gives him the chance to reply with "I thought we were working on it together, I'm sorry if that wasn't clear," which is both plausible and devastating to a 600-word email.

What I'd do instead, in order:

1. Nothing today. Close the draft. Go for a walk. Do not look at it again until tomorrow.

2. Tomorrow, talk to him. Directly, briefly, in person or by call. "That was my framing from the doc I shared with you last week. You presented it as yours and didn't mention me. I need you to correct that with [manager] and the VPs." No preamble, no essay. Watch what he does. If he corrects it, you got what you needed and he knows you noticed. If he deflects, you now have a second data point for step 3.

3. Your manager, one to one. Bring the doc with the timestamp. "I want you to know where that idea came from, and I want it credited. Here is the doc from last week. I've spoken to him and asked him to correct it. If he doesn't, I'd like your help making sure the VPs know." This gives your manager the chance to fix it without being embarrassed, and puts the next move in their hands, which is where it belongs organisationally.

4. If he and your manager both do nothing, then a short note to the VPs is on the table, and it should be two paragraphs, factual, with the doc attached, and sent by you or ideally forwarded by your manager. Not 600 words. Not with your heart rate up.

In the meantime, keep the draft. Writing it did something useful; it got the feeling out. It just shouldn't be what they read.

I'll give you ways to fit it in, but I want to say the other thing first, because I think you already know it: you cannot keep doing twenty minutes a day for six children on your lunch break for the rest of the year. Not because it isn't worth it. Because you will break, and then those six kids have no one. Running on fumes in October with eight months to go is not a scheduling problem, it is the system quietly putting a district-level failure on your plate and calling it dedication.

So, two kinds of answer.

Ways to get the adult-at-the-table time without it being you every day:

1. Cross-age tutors. Fifth graders, trained in a half-hour session on how to do paired reading and a few prompts, can sit with a second grader for 15 to 20 minutes three times a week. The research on this is good for both children. Ask a fifth-grade teacher if they'd release a handful of kids during their independent reading. It costs nothing and it is the single most scalable thing on this list.

2. Volunteers. Reading Partners, AARP Foundation Experience Corps, local retirees, church groups, a parent who works from home. One reliable volunteer two mornings a week is two of your six lunches back. Your principal or office manager may already have a list.

3. Rotate inside the flexible block, even if it is nominally test prep. If the rest of the class is doing test prep independently or in pairs, you sit with two of the six for ten minutes, then the next two. Nobody can object to you being with children during a block designated for literacy work, and "test prep" for a child who can't yet read is reading instruction anyway. Call it what they want it called.

4. Morning. If your school has any window between arrival and the bell, or if the six come to breakfast, ten minutes then is better than nothing and keeps your lunch yours.

5. Make the ask of the specialist specific. "Can you take my six for twenty minutes on the two days you are here" is easier to say yes to than "can you help." Even two days a week halves your load.

The other answer is about the district. You are a teacher doing a reading specialist's job unpaid at lunch because the district spread one specialist across four schools and reassigned your intervention time. Write down what you are doing, for how many kids, how many minutes, since when, and what it is costing you. Give that to your principal in writing, not as a complaint but as data: "Six of my 27 cannot yet decode. I am providing 20 minutes daily on my own time. This is not sustainable past December. What is the plan?" Principals can sometimes move things when a teacher gives them the numbers and the deadline.

And please take three lunches a week back now, before the two you are still giving stop being a choice. The children need you in March more than they need you at 12:15 on a Thursday.

Here is the position in England, Wales and Scotland, and you can check it at gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights:

- The statutory minimum is 5.6 weeks' paid holiday a year, which for someone working five days a week is 28 days.
- There is no statutory right to bank holidays off, and no statutory right to be paid extra for them.
- An employer can count bank holidays as part of the 5.6 weeks. For a full-time worker, that means 20 days plus the 8 bank holidays equals the 28-day minimum. That is extremely common in hospitality, and it is lawful.

So you are not required to give eight extra days on top of 28. What your sister-in-law may be thinking of is that many employers, particularly in office jobs, give 25 days plus bank holidays as a matter of policy, which is more generous than the minimum. Or she may be thinking of a contract that promises bank holidays in addition, in which case that contract is binding. But that is a contractual promise, not a legal floor.

Two things to check before you talk to your staff:

1. What the existing contracts say. If any current contract or offer letter promises "28 days plus bank holidays," you have to honour it for those staff regardless of the statutory position.
2. Part-timers and anyone working variable hours. Their entitlement is pro rata, and if bank holidays fall on days they don't work, the way you count them can produce unfairness; ACAS has guidance on this and it is worth reading.

On the staff who are upset: they have seen a draft that gives them the legal minimum, and someone they trust has told them they are being short-changed. The fact that they aren't legally short-changed will not, on its own, make that feeling go away. You might want to say something like: "The contracts give 28 days including bank holidays, which is the legal minimum and standard in cafés. I've checked and it's correct. I know that's not the same as what some office jobs offer. If the business can afford more later I'd like to, but I'm not going to promise what I can't keep." That's honest, and it is better than either retracting a correct contract or pretending the minimum is generous.

If you'd like to give more than the minimum and can afford it, that is a perfectly good decision, just make it as a decision, not because of a mistaken belief about the law.

If you want certainty from someone other than me, the ACAS helpline (0300 123 1100) is free and will confirm this in two minutes. I'd genuinely encourage you to call them, both for your own peace of mind and so you can tell your staff you've checked with ACAS, which carries more weight than either me or a family member.

What you're feeling is relief, and relief is the correct response to four years of carrying something very heavy and then setting it down. It doesn't mean you didn't love her. It means it was heavy.

People who have been carers for a long time very often describe exactly this: the sleep, the quiet, the sudden lightness, and then the guilt about the lightness, or in your case the waiting for guilt that doesn't come. The waiting is the part that's worth looking at. You seem to think the real feeling is the terrible one and the fine one is a kind of mistake that will be corrected. I'd suggest it is the other way round. Your body slept for eleven hours because it finally could. The quiet house feels good because for four years it never was quiet. That is information about what the four years cost you, not about what kind of person you are.

It also doesn't mean nothing else will come. Grief and relief aren't in competition. You may feel a wave of something at an odd moment: a cup in the cupboard, the first weekend you don't have to plan around her, the first time she doesn't know where she is when you visit. Or you may not, and that would also be fine. There's no required amount of feeling terrible, and you don't earn the right to have done a hard thing by suffering about it afterwards.

On telling everyone it was a hard day: it was. Moving a parent into a care home after four years at home is a hard day whether or not it felt hard. You're not lying. But if you'd like to try saying the true thing to one person, "honestly, I feel lighter than I have in years and it's strange," I think you'll find more people than you expect say "yes, me too." Carers' groups are full of people who know exactly this feeling and don't judge it.

One gentle thing to watch for over the next few weeks: not guilt, but the loss of the role. Four years of being needed every day leaves a shape, and sometimes it's a few weeks before you notice the gap where the purpose was. If that comes, it's not a sign you got it wrong either.

You did a hard thing well and for a long time. Being fine afterwards is allowed.

Yes. Here is a clinical explanation pitched for a family, followed by some notes on delivering it, since the questions families ask in this situation are usually about suffering and about whether anything could have been done.

What happens in a fentanyl overdose

Fentanyl is an opioid, and like all opioids it acts on receptors in the brain and brainstem. At high doses its main effect is on the part of the brainstem that drives breathing. The sequence is usually:

1. Sedation. Within minutes of a large dose, often much faster with fentanyl than with heroin or oxycodone, the person becomes very drowsy and then unconscious. With fentanyl this can happen in seconds to a few minutes. Many people lose consciousness very quickly, sometimes before they have finished what they were doing.

2. Respiratory depression. The brainstem's drive to breathe is suppressed. Breathing becomes slow and shallow, then irregular, then stops. The person is unconscious by this stage. They are not aware of struggling for breath; the sensation of air hunger comes from the same brain systems that opioids suppress, so the person does not experience the suffocating feeling that someone drowning or choking would.

3. Hypoxia. With breathing stopped, oxygen in the blood falls over a few minutes. Lips and fingertips may turn blue or grey. The heart, deprived of oxygen, slows and eventually stops. Brain injury begins after about four to six minutes without oxygen, and death follows if breathing is not restored.

The whole process, from dose to death, can take as little as a few minutes with fentanyl, and it is often faster than with other opioids, which is part of why so many deaths occur before anyone can intervene. In other cases, particularly where some breathing continues, it can be slower, over an hour or more.

What the person experienced

This is what families most want to know. The honest answer is that opioid overdose is, as far as we can tell, not painful and not frightening for the person. They become sleepy and lose consciousness, and everything after that happens while they are unaware. The signs that are distressing to witness, the blue colour, the gurgling or snoring sound of obstructed breathing, the stillness, are happening to someone who is not aware of them. They did not feel themselves stop breathing, and they were not in pain.

What the family may also ask

- Could naloxone have helped? Naloxone reverses opioid effects and restores breathing if given while the heart is still beating. With fentanyl, the window is short and higher or repeated doses are often needed. If no one was there, or no one had naloxone, there was often no realistic window, and that is not the family's fault.
- Did they know what they were taking? Fentanyl is frequently present in drugs sold as something else, and in doses the person could not have known about. Many fentanyl deaths are in people who had no idea it was there.
- Did they suffer for a long time? Usually not. See above.

Delivering it

- Ask first what they already understand and what they most want to know. Some want the mechanism; some only want to know whether their person was in pain.
- Use the word "died." Avoid "passed" or "lost."
- Lead with the fact that the person was unconscious and not in pain; it is the information that matters most and they may not absorb much after it.
- Avoid words that imply blame or choice: say "the dose was more than the body could handle," not "they took too much."
- Leave silence. Let them ask.
- Have the name of a bereavement service for families affected by drug deaths ready; in the UK that is DrugFAM or Cruse, in the US it can be GRASP or local peer groups.

Good instinct to check before confronting her. Here's how to do it properly, in about an hour, and it's all free. You'll need his full name, the firm name he uses, and ideally the city.

1. FINRA BrokerCheck (brokercheck.finra.org). Search his name. This covers anyone licensed to sell securities, current or former. It shows registrations, employment history, exams passed, and crucially any disclosures: customer complaints, regulatory actions, terminations, bankruptcies, criminal matters. If he claims to manage a portfolio and he's not here or on the next site, that's a serious problem in itself.

2. SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (adviserinfo.sec.gov). Search his name and the firm. This covers registered investment advisers and their representatives. It shows the firm's Form ADV, which lists who runs it, assets under management, disciplinary history, and how they get paid. Read Part 2 of the ADV if the firm exists; it's written in plain English.

3. Arizona Corporation Commission, Securities Division (azcc.gov/securities). Arizona licenses securities salespeople and advisers at state level, and this is where you check that he's actually allowed to do this in Tucson. They have a search and a phone line, 602-542-0662. Ask them directly: is this person licensed, is this firm registered, and are there any complaints or enforcement actions. They will tell you.

4. Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions (difi.az.gov). If what he's selling is an annuity or life insurance, which is common in these situations, that's an insurance license, not a securities one, and this is where it's checked. Church-sourced advisers to older people very often turn out to be insurance agents selling high-commission annuities, which may be legal and still be bad for her.

5. The firm. Search the Arizona Corporation Commission business entity database (ecorp.azcc.gov) to see if the firm exists as a registered entity, who the officers are, and when it was formed. Then search the firm name in BrokerCheck and IAPD. A firm that exists as an LLC but isn't registered with the SEC, FINRA or the state cannot lawfully manage investments.

6. The person. Plain web search of his name plus "Tucson," "complaint," "lawsuit," "fraud." Pima County Superior Court case lookup (search public records at sc.pima.gov). Check whether the name on his business card is the name on his licence.

7. Where the money actually went. If she wrote cheques or did transfers, the payee tells you a lot. Money that went to a custodian like Schwab, Fidelity or a named insurance company is in a very different place from money that went to him personally or to his LLC. If you can see even one statement, that's the most important document you have.

Two things to be ready for:

- He may check out. Licensed, no complaints, real firm. That doesn't make the arrangement good. Affinity-based selling through churches is a well-known channel for products that are legal and terrible: annuities with fifteen-year surrender periods, high-fee funds, unsuitable concentration. If he's licensed, the next question is what she's actually been put into and what it would cost to get out.
- He may not check out. In that case, don't confront him, and don't tell your mum you're going to the authorities before you've done it; she may warn him. Report to the Arizona Corporation Commission Securities Division and to Arizona Adult Protective Services (1-877-767-2385). APS exists exactly for financial exploitation of older adults and can act even when she's unwilling. The FTC and FINRA also take reports.

On talking to her afterwards: the defensiveness is the fraud working, if it is one. The people who do this invest heavily in being trusted and liked, and they often tell the client that family will try to interfere. When you go back to her, lead with what you found, not with what you think of him, and frame it as protecting her money rather than questioning her judgement. Something like "I looked him up and I want to show you what I found, and then you decide."
